section.heading: 10.3. Polar Coordinates
section.paragraph: A coordinate system represents a point in the plane by an ordered pair of numbers called coordinates. Usually we use Cartesian coordinates, which are directed distances from two perpendicular axes. Here we describe a coordinate system introduced by Newton, called the polar coordinate system, which is more convenient for many purposes.
section.heading: The Polar Coordinate System
section.paragraph: We choose a point in the plane that is called the pole (or origin) and is labeled $$O$$ . Then we draw a ray (half-line) starting at $$O$$ called the polar axis. This axis is usually drawn horizontally to the right and corresponds to the positive $$x$$ -axis in Cartesian coordinates.

If $$P$$ is any other point in the plane, let $$r$$ be the distance from $$O$$ to $$P$$ and let $$\theta$$ be the angle (usually measured in radians) between the polar axis and the line $$OP$$ as in Figure 1. Then the point $$P$$ is represented by the ordered pair $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ and $$r$$ , $$\theta$$ are called polar coordinates of $$P$$ . We use the convention that an angle is positive if measured in the counterclockwise direction from the polar axis and negative in the clockwise direction. If $$P = O$$ , then $$r = 0$$ and we agree that $$\left( {0,\theta} \right)$$ represents the pole for any value of $$\theta$$ .

image.alt: Details A point, a ray, and a line segment. A point located at the bottom left is labeled O. A ray labeled x runs horizontally rightward from O. The ray is also labeled polar axis. The line segment is labeled r, begins at O, slopes upward to the right at an angle theta measured counterclockwise from the polar axis, and ends at a point labeled P(r, theta).

section.paragraph: We extend the meaning of polar coordinates $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ to the case in which $$r$$ is negative by agreeing that, as in Figure 2, the points $$\left( {- r,\theta} \right)$$ and $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ lie on the same line through $$O$$ and at the same distance $$|r|$$ from $$O$$ , but on opposite sides of $$O$$ . If $$r > 0$$ , the point $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ lies in the same quadrant as $$\theta$$ ; if $$r < 0$$ , it lies in the quadrant on the opposite side of the pole. Notice that $$\left( {- r,\theta} \right)$$ represents the same point as $$\left( {r,\theta + \pi} \right)$$ .

The first line segment begins from O, slopes upward to the right at an angle theta measured counterclockwise from the horizontal ray and ends at a point labeled (r, theta). A dashed line segment begins from O and mirrors the first line segment. It slopes down to the left and ends at a point labeled (negative r, theta). The dashed line segment is at an angle theta + pi, measured counterclockwise, from the horizontal ray.

section.paragraph: In the Cartesian coordinate system every point has only one representation, but in the polar coordinate system each point has many representations. For instance, the point $$\left( {1,5\pi \slash 4} \right)$$ in Example 1(a) could be written as $$\left( {1, - 3\pi \slash 4} \right)$$ or $$\left( {1,13\pi \slash 4} \right)$$ or $$\left( {- 1,\pi \slash 4} \right)$$ . (See Figure 4.)

section.paragraph: In fact, since a complete counterclockwise rotation is given by an angle $$2\pi$$ , the point represented by polar coordinates $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ is also represented by
$$\left( {r,\theta + 2n\pi} \right)$$
and
$$\left( {- r,\theta + (2n + 1)\pi} \right)$$
where $$n$$ is any integer.
section.heading: Relationship between Polar and Cartesian Coordinates
section.paragraph: The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates can be seen from Figure 5, in which the pole corresponds to the origin and the polar axis coincides with the positive $$x$$ -axis. If the point $$P$$ has Cartesian coordinates $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and polar coordinates $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ , then, from the figure, we have $$\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r}$$ and $$\sin\theta = \frac{y}{r}$$ . So to find the Cartesian coordinates $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ when the polar coordinates $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ are known, we use the equations
$$x = r\cos\theta y = r\sin\theta$$

image.alt: Details Two line segments are graphed on the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The first line segment, labeled r, begins at the origin, slopes upward to the right at an angle theta from the positive x-axis, and ends at a point labeled P(r, theta) = P(x, y). From this point, a vertical line segment, labeled y, descends downward and meets the x-axis at 90 degrees. The distance between the origin and the point where the vertical line segment meets the x-axis is labeled x.

section.paragraph: To find polar coordinates $$(r,\theta)$$ when the Cartesian coordinates $$(x,y)$$ are known, we use the equations
which can be deduced from Equations 1 or simply read from Figure 5.

Although Equations 1 and 2 were deduced from Figure 5, which illustrates the case where $$r > 0$$ and $$0 < \theta < \pi \slash 2$$ , these equations are valid for all values of $$r$$ and $$\theta$$ . (See the general definition of $$\sin\theta$$ and $$\cos\theta$$ in Appendix D.)

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Convert the point $$\left( {2,\pi \slash 3} \right)$$ from polar to Cartesian coordinates.
Solution Since $$r = 2$$ and $$\theta = \pi \slash 3$$ , Equations 1 give
$$\begin{array}{l} {x = r\cos\theta = 2\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 1} \\ {y = r\sin\theta = 2\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = 2 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sqrt{3}} \end{array}$$
Therefore the point is $$\left( {1,\sqrt{3}} \right)$$ in Cartesian coordinates.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Represent the point with Cartesian coordinates $$\left( {1, - 1} \right)$$ in terms of polar coordinates.
Solution If we choose $$r$$ to be positive, then Equations 2 give
$$\begin{array}{rcl} r & = & {\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} = \sqrt{1^{2} + \left( {- 1} \right)^{2}} = \sqrt{2}} \\ {\tan\theta} & = & {\frac{y}{x} = - 1} \end{array}$$

Since the point $$\left( {1, - 1} \right)$$ lies in the fourth quadrant, we can choose $$\theta = - \pi \slash 4$$ or $$\theta = 7\pi \slash 4$$ . Thus one possible answer is $$\left( {\sqrt{2}, - \pi \slash 4} \right)$$ ; another is $$\left( {\sqrt{2},7\pi \slash 4} \right)$$ .

section.paragraph: Note Equations 2 do not uniquely determine $$\theta$$ when $$x$$ and $$y$$ are given because, as $$\theta$$ increases through the interval $$0 \leqslant \theta < 2\pi$$ , each value of $$\tan\theta$$ occurs twice. Therefore, in converting from Cartesian to polar coordinates, it’s not good enough just to find $$r$$ and $$\theta$$ that satisfy Equations 2. As in Example 3, we must choose $$\theta$$ so that the point $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ lies in the correct quadrant.
section.heading: Polar Curves
section.paragraph: The graph of a polar equation $$r = f(\theta)$$ , or more generally $$F\left( {r,\theta} \right) = 0$$ , consists of all points $$P$$ that have at least one polar representation $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ whose coordinates satisfy the equation.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: What curve is represented by the polar equation $$r = 2$$ ?

Solution The curve consists of all points $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ with $$r = 2$$ . Since $$r$$ represents the distance from the point to the pole, the curve $$r = 2$$ represents the circle with center $$O$$ and radius $$2$$ . In general, the equation $$r = a$$ represents a circle with center $$O$$ and radius $$|a|$$ . (See Figure 6.)

image.alt: Details Four concentric circles, centered on the origin, are graphed on the positive x-axis. The first and innermost circle is labeled r = 1/2. The next circle is labeled r = 1. The third circle is labeled r = 2. The fourth and outermost circle is labeled r = 4. A ray labeled x begins from the origin and extends rightward.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Sketch the polar curve $$\theta = 1$$ .

Solution This curve consists of all points $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ such that the polar angle $$\theta$$ is $$1$$ radian. It is the straight line that passes through $$O$$ and makes an angle of $$1$$ radian with the polar axis (see Figure 7). Notice that the points $$\left( {r,1} \right)$$ on the line with $$r > 0$$ are in the first quadrant, whereas those with $$r < 0$$ are in the third quadrant.

The line slopes upward to the right, passing through the points labeled (negative 2, 1), (negative 1, 1), O, (1, 1), (2, 1), and (3, 1). The line is labeled theta = 1 and is at an angle theta, measured counterclockwise, from the horizontal ray.

example.heading: Example 6

list.item: (a) Sketch the curve with polar equation $$r = 2\cos\theta$$ .
(b) Find a Cartesian equation for this curve.

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) In Figure 8 we find the values of $$r$$ for some convenient values of $$\theta$$ and plot the corresponding points $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ . Then we join these points to sketch the curve, which appears to be a circle. We have used only values of $$\theta$$ between $$0$$ and $$\pi$$ , because if we let $$\theta$$ increase beyond $$\pi$$ , we obtain the same points again. Figure 8 Details The figure has two parts. The first part is a table with two columns and nine rows. The column headers are theta and r = 2 cos(theta). The data provided in the table are as follows: Row 1: 0, 2. Row 2: pi/6, sqrt(3). Row 3: pi/4, sqrt(2). Row 4: pi/3, 1. Row 5: pi/2, 0. Row 6: 2 pi/3, negative 1. Row 7: 3 pi/4, negative sqrt(2). Row 8: 5 pi/6, negative sqrt(3). Row 9: pi, negative 2. In the second part, a circle and six line segments are graphed on a coordinate plane. The circle is divided into two halves by the positive horizontal axis and passes through six points labeled (0, pi/2), located at the origin, (1, pi/3), (sqrt(2), pi/4), (sqrt(3), pi/6), (2, 0), located on the horizontal axis, (negative sqrt(3), 3 pi/6), (negative sqrt(2), 3 pi/4), (negative 1, 2 pi/3). From (0, pi/2), three dashed line segments slope upward to the right until the points (1, pi/3), (sqrt(2), pi/4), and (sqrt(3), pi/6). From (0, pi/2), three dashed line segments slope downward to the right until the points (negative sqrt(3), 3 pi/6), (negative sqrt(2), 3 pi/4), and (negative 1, 2 pi/3). The three line segments that slope downward are extended beyond the point (0, pi/2). Table of values and graph of $$r = 2\cos\theta$$

(b) To convert the given equation to a Cartesian equation we use Equations 1 and 2. From $$x = r\cos\theta$$ we have $$\cos\theta = x \slash r$$ , so the equation $$r = 2\cos\theta$$ becomes $$r = 2x \slash r$$ , which gives $$2x = r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ or $$x^{2} + y^{2} - 2x = 0$$ Completing the square, we obtain $$\left( {x - 1} \right)^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ which is an equation of a circle with center $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ and radius $$1$$ .

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Sketch the curve $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ .

Solution Instead of plotting points as in Example 6, we first sketch the graph of $$r = 1 + \sin\theta$$ in Cartesian coordinates in Figure 10 by shifting the sine curve up one unit. This enables us to read at a glance the values of $$r$$ that correspond to increasing values of $$\theta$$ . For instance, we see that as $$\theta$$ increases from $$0$$ to $$\pi \slash 2$$ , $$r$$ (the distance from $$O$$ ) increases from $$1$$ to $$2$$ (see the corresponding green arrows in Figures 10 and 11), so we sketch the corresponding part of the polar curve in Figure 11(a). As $$\theta$$ increases from $$\pi \slash 2$$ to $$\pi$$ , Figure 10 shows that $$r$$ decreases from $$2$$ to $$1$$ , so we sketch the next part of the curve as in Figure 11(b). As $$\theta$$ increases from $$\pi$$ to $$3\pi \slash 2$$ , $$r$$ decreases from $$1$$ to $$0$$ as shown in part (c). Finally, as $$\theta$$ increases from $$3\pi \slash 2$$ to $$2\pi$$ , $$r$$ increases from $$0$$ to $$1$$ as shown in part (d). If we let $$\theta$$ increase beyond $$2\pi$$ or decrease beyond $$0$$ , we would simply retrace this path. Putting together the parts of the curve from Figure 11(a)–(d), we sketch the complete curve in part (e). It is called a cardioid because it’s shaped like a heart.

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Sketch the curve $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ .

Solution As in Example 7, we first sketch $$r = \cos 2\theta$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , in Cartesian coordinates in Figure 12. As $$\theta$$ increases from $$0$$ to $$\pi \slash 4$$ , Figure 12 shows that $$r$$ decreases from $$1$$ to $$0$$ and so we draw the corresponding portion of the polar curve in Figure 13 (indicated by ①). As $$\theta$$ increases from $$\pi \slash 4$$ to $$\pi \slash 2$$ , $$r$$ decreases from $$0$$ to $$- 1$$ . This means that the distance from $$O$$ increases from $$0$$ to $$1$$ , but instead of being in the first quadrant this portion of the polar curve (indicated by ②) lies on the opposite side of the pole in the third quadrant. The remainder of the curve is drawn in a similar fashion, with the arrows and numbers indicating the order in which the portions are traced out. The resulting curve has four loops and is called a four-leaved rose.

section.heading: Symmetry
section.paragraph: When we sketch polar curves it is sometimes helpful to take advantage of symmetry. The following three rules are explained by Figure 14.

image.alt: Details A closed curve and three line segments are drawn on a horizontal line. The horizontal line has a point labeled O and the curve is symmetric about the horizontal line. The curve has a large almost circular arc on the right, leading to a narrow neck near point O, followed by a small almost circular arc bulging leftward. From O, a line segment slopes upward to the right at an angle theta measured counterclockwise from O and reaches the right side of the curve at a point labeled (r, theta). From O, another line segment slopes downward to the right at an angle theta measured clockwise from O and reaches the right side of the curve at a point labeled (r, negative theta). A vertical dashed line segment connects the two points on the right side of the curve. A closed curve with two loops is graphed on a coordinate plane. The curve resembles an infinity symbol with the two loops in the first and third quadrants. A line segment slopes upward to the right passing through the origin and connects a point labeled (negative r, theta) located on the upper half of the loop in the third quadrant to a point labeled (r, theta) located on the lower half of the loop in the first quadrant. A closed curve and three line segments are drawn on a coordinate plane. The curve is symmetric about the vertical axis. The top portion of the curve is horizontal and concave down, which then tapers downward on both sides to a broad neck near the origin, labeled O, and opens into a small bowl-like curve with a rounded base. From O, a line segment slopes upward to the right at an angle theta measured counterclockwise from O and reaches the right side of the curve at a point labeled (r, theta). From O, another line segment slopes upward to the left at an angle pi minus theta measured counterclockwise from O and reaches the left side of the curve at a point labeled (r, negative theta). A horizontal dashed line segment connects the two points.

list.item: (a) If a polar equation is unchanged when $$\theta$$ is replaced by $$- \theta$$ , the curve is symmetric about the polar axis.

(b) If the equation is unchanged when $$r$$ is replaced by $$- r$$ , or when $$\theta$$ is replaced by $$\theta + \pi$$ , the curve is symmetric about the pole. (This means that the curve remains unchanged if we rotate it through $$180^{{^\circ}}$$ about the origin.)
(c) If the equation is unchanged when $$\theta$$ is replaced by $$\pi - \theta$$ , the curve is symmetric about the vertical line $$\theta = \pi \slash 2$$ .

section.paragraph: The curves sketched in Examples 6 and 8 are symmetric about the polar axis, since $$\cos\left( {- \theta} \right) = \cos\theta$$ . The curves in Examples 7 and 8 are symmetric about $$\theta = \pi \slash 2$$ because $$\sin\left( {\pi - \theta} \right) = \sin\theta$$ and $$\cos\left\lbrack 2{\left( {\pi - \theta} \right)\rbrack} = \cos 2\theta \right.$$ . The four-leaved rose is also symmetric about the pole. We could have used these symmetry properties in sketching the curves. For instance, in Example 6 we need only have plotted points for $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi \slash 2$$ and then reflected about the polar axis to obtain the complete circle.
section.heading: Graphing Polar Curves with Technology
section.paragraph: Although it’s useful to be able to sketch simple polar curves by hand, we need to use a graphing calculator or computer when we are faced with a curve as complicated as the ones shown in Figures 15 and 16.

Two petals are along the positive and negative horizontal axis, symmetric about them. The remaining 8 petals are located two in each quadrant. A wavy circle is drawn around the flower such that the high points of the wave coincide with the rounded ends of the petals.

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Graph the curve $$r = \sin\left( {8\theta \slash 5} \right)$$ .
Solution First we need to determine the domain for $$\theta$$ . So we ask ourselves: how many complete rotations are required until the curve starts to repeat itself? If the answer is $$n$$ , then
$$\sin\frac{8\left( {\theta + 2n\pi} \right)}{5} = \sin\left( {\frac{8\theta}{5} + \frac{16n\pi}{5}} \right) = \sin\frac{8\theta}{5}$$

and so we require that $$16n\pi \slash 5$$ be an even multiple of $$\pi$$ . This will first occur when $$n = 5$$ . Therefore we will graph the entire curve if we specify that $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 10\pi$$ . Figure 17 shows the resulting curve. Notice that this curve has $$16$$ loops.

image.alt: Details A function is graphed in a graphing calculator window. Both the axes are displayed from negative 1 to 1. The function resembles a flower with many overlapping petals.

example.heading: Example 10
example.paragraph: Investigate the family of polar curves given by $$r = 1 + c\sin\theta$$ . How does the shape change as $$c$$ changes? (These curves are called limaçons, after a French word for snail, because of the shape of the curves for certain values of $$c$$ .)

Solution Figure 18 shows computer-drawn graphs for various values of $$c$$ . (Note that we obtain the complete graph for $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ .) For $$c > 1$$ there is a loop that decreases in size as $$c$$ decreases. When $$c = 1$$ the loop disappears and the curve becomes the cardioid that we sketched in Example 7. For $$c$$ between $$1$$ and $$\frac{1}{2}$$ the cardioid’s cusp is smoothed out and becomes a “dimple.” When $$c$$ decreases from $$\frac{1}{2}$$ to $$0$$ , the limaçon is shaped like an oval. This oval becomes more circular as $$\left. c\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , and when $$c = 0$$ the curve is just the circle $$r = 1$$ .

example.paragraph: In Exercise 55 you are asked to prove analytically what we have discovered from the graphs in Figure 18.

The remaining parts of Figure 18 show that as $$c$$ becomes negative, the shapes change in reverse order. In fact, these curves are reflections about the horizontal axis of the corresponding curves with positive $$c$$ .

section.paragraph: Limaçons arise in the study of planetary motion. In particular, the trajectory of Mars, as viewed from the planet Earth, has been modeled by a limaçon with a loop, as in the parts of Figure 18 with $$|c| > 1$$ .

section.heading: Discovery Project Families of Polar Curves
section.paragraph: In this project you will discover the interesting and beautiful shapes that members of families of polar curves can take. You will also see how the shape of the curve changes when you vary the constants.

list.item: (a) Investigate the family of curves defined by the polar equations $$r = \sin n\theta$$ , where $$n$$ is a positive integer. How is the number of loops related to $$n$$ ? (b) What happens if the equation in part (a) is replaced by $$r = \left| {\sin n\theta} \right|$$ ?

A family of curves is given by the equations $$r = 1 + c\sin n\theta$$ , where $$c$$ is a real number and $$n$$ is a positive integer. How does the graph change as $$n$$ increases? How does it change as $$c$$ changes? Illustrate by graphing enough members of the family to support your conclusions.

A family of curves has polar equations $$r = \frac{1 - a\cos\theta}{1 + a\cos\theta}$$ Investigate how the graph changes as the number $$a$$ changes. In particular, you should identify the transitional values of $$a$$ for which the basic shape of the curve changes.

The astronomer Giovanni Cassini (1625–1712) studied the family of curves with polar equations $$r^{4} - 2c^{ 2}r^{2}\cos 2\theta + c^{4} - a^{4} = 0$$ where $$a$$ and $$c$$ are positive real numbers. These curves are called the ovals of Cassini even though they are oval shaped only for certain values of $$a$$ and $$c$$ . (Cassini thought that these curves might represent planetary orbits better than Kepler’s ellipses.) Investigate the variety of shapes that these curves may have. In particular, how are $$a$$ and $$c$$ related to each other when the curve splits into two parts?
